namespace Erdos897

/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$ such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n (f(n+1)−f(n))/ \log n = ∞$?

The answer is no; this follows from a construction of Wirsing [Wi81], rediscovered by
Archivara [Ar25] and formalised in Lean by Aristotle [ArWu25].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos897.lean"]
theorem erdos_897.parts.i : answer(False) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b) →
    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => ((f (n+1) - f n) / (n : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n f(n+1)/ f(n) = ∞$?

The answer is no; the same counterexample is formalised in Lean by Aristotle [ArWu25].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos897.lean"]
theorem erdos_897.parts.ii : answer(False) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b) →
    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => (f (n+1) / f n : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/--
Wirsing [Wi70] proved that if $|f(n+1)−f(n)| ≤ C$ then $f(n) = c \log n + O(1)$ for some constant
$c$. This is Erdős Problem 491; see `erdos_491`, whose linked formal proof gives this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos491.lean#L34"]
theorem erdos_897.variants.log_growth
    (f : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hf : ∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b)
    (C : ℝ) (hf' : ∀ n, |f (n+1) - f n| ≤ C) :
    ∃ c, ∃ (O : ℕ → ℝ), O =O[Filter.atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧
      ∀ n, f n ≤ c*Real.log n + O n := by
  sorry


/--

if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$ and $f(p^k) = f(p)$
or $f(p^k) = kf(p)$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n (f(n+1)−f(n))/ \log n = ∞$?

The known counterexample does not satisfy either of these extra hypotheses, so this variant remains

  sorry

/--

findings.description: The growth hypothesis uses `atTop` on `ℕ × ℕ`, so both p and k must become arbitrarily large. This is stronger than unboundedness over prime powers p^k as p^k → ∞: it discards every fixed prime and every bounded exponent. For example, the additive function f(n)=v₂(n)² has f(2^k)/log(2^k)=k/log 2, hence the source's prime-power limsup is +∞, but the written filter sees an eventually zero function once p≥3. These facts were checked in Lean. The known counterexample satisfies both growth conditions, so the negative answer remains correct, but the hypothesis does not express the source's condition.
findings.source_evidence: Archivara, An Additive Counterexample: Erdős Problem 897, abstract and §1, describes a function 'arbitrarily large on prime powers relative to log'. In §3, Lemma 1, the proof explicitly discusses q→∞, including 'for instance along q=2^m as m→∞', and calls this the 'limsup over prime powers'. https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741
findings.suggested_fix: Take the limsup over the sizes of prime powers: `(Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}).limsup (fun q => (f q / Real.log (q : ℝ) : EReal)) = ⊤`. Alternatively, express unboundedness as `∀ M : ℝ, ∃ p k : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ 0 < k ∧ M < f (p^k) / Real.log ((p : ℝ)^k)`.

findings.description: The same product-`atTop` growth hypothesis requires unbounded normalized values with both p and k large, rather than over all large prime powers. It excludes legitimate source inputs such as f(n)=v₂(n)²: its normalized values tend to +∞ on powers of 2, while its limsup under the written filter is zero. Thus the ratio question is posed with a strictly stronger growth hypothesis. This is separate from the correctly recorded negative answer.
findings.source_evidence: The ratio question in §1 of the cited Archivara paper has the same prime-power growth assumption as the consecutive-difference question. §3 interprets the growth over q=p^k→∞ and explicitly includes powers of the fixed prime 2. https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the product filter by `Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}` and use `f q / Real.log (q : ℝ)`, as for part i.

findings.description: The conclusion only requires `f n ≤ c * Real.log n + O n` with O bounded. It does not require the residual f(n)−c log n to be bounded below, and therefore states only a one-sided logarithmic upper bound, not the asserted logarithmic main term with bounded error. The conclusions are different even on additive functions: −v₂(n)² satisfies the written conclusion with c=0 and O=0, but has no bounded logarithmic residual. This separation was proved in Lean; that example is not a counterexample to Wirsing's bounded-gap theorem.
findings.source_evidence: The cited formal proof, `erdos_491`, concludes `∃ c, (fun n => f n - c * Real.log n) =O[atTop] (fun _ => 1)`; its `logarithmic_uniform_bound` bounds `|f n - c * Real.log n|`. https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos491.lean#L34. Independently, Erdős, Some of my favourite problems which recently have been solved (1982), p.65, §5, states f(n)=c₁ log n+g(n) with |g(n)| bounded and attributes its proof to Wirsing: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1982-33.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `f n ≤ c * Real.log n + O n` by equality. Equivalently, conclude `∃ c : ℝ, (fun n : ℕ => f n - c * Real.log (n : ℝ)) =O[Filter.atTop] (fun _ : ℕ => (1 : ℝ))`.

findings.description: The first disjunct, `∀ k p, p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p`, includes k=0. Additivity gives f(1)=0, so k=0 forces f(p)=0 for every prime; the remaining equations then force f(p^k)=0 for every prime power. This contradicts the limsup hypothesis. Consequently the entire strongly additive alternative is vacuous, and the question reduces to the completely additive alternative alone. I proved this reduction for an arbitrary conclusion in Lean. I also checked that the genuine strongly additive function ∑_{p∣n}p² satisfies the written growth hypothesis but is excluded by both written disjuncts.
findings.source_evidence: The variant's docstring, lines 86–93, identifies the intended alternative as f(p^k)=f(p). The accessible cited paper explicitly takes prime powers with positive exponent: 'For each prime power q=p^k with k≥1' (Archivara, §2.1, p.2, https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741). Extending that identity to p^0=1 changes its meaning. The live website's variant paragraph could not be independently retrieved; this limitation is recorded below.
findings.suggested_fix: Require a positive exponent in the first disjunct, e.g. `∀ (k p : ℕ), 0 < k → p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p`. For consistency, both alternatives may quantify only over positive k; the k=0 case of the completely additive alternative is already implied by additivity.

findings.description: The strongly additive alternative again quantifies over k=0. Together with additivity this forces all prime-power values to vanish, contradicting the growth hypothesis. Thus this declaration omits the intended strongly additive ratio question and only tests the completely additive case. The whole theorem is not vacuous—only the first alternative disappears.
findings.source_evidence: The variant's docstring, lines 104–111, includes the alternative f(p^k)=f(p). The cited Archivara paper's prime-power convention is explicitly k≥1 (§2.1, p.2): https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741. The live source's variant wording was inaccessible, but the k=0 contradiction and loss of the advertised class were verified in Lean.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `0 < k` to the first disjunct's hypotheses, or quantify both power-law alternatives over positive exponents.

review.notes: Three distinct issues affect five declarations. The accessible counterexample paper, external Lean proof, and independent status database support the two negative answers; no confirmed stale status was found. The product-filter issue is not separately reported for the variants: under either intended positive-exponent power law, unboundedness over prime powers is equivalent to the joint-filter +∞ condition. Positive-input coprime additivity is also equivalent to the all-natural-input version used in the cited proof; this equivalence was checked in Lean. Boundary tests and diagnostic proofs are in /workspace/review/verified_checks.lean, which compiled without errors. demonstrated.claim: The literal growth hypothesis rejects the additive function f(n)=v₂(n)², although its normalized values along powers of 2 tend to +∞.
The same literal product-filter growth hypothesis rejects f(n)=v₂(n)² despite its unbounded normalized prime-power growth.

The first power-law disjunct contradicts additivity and the growth hypothesis because k=0 forces all prime-power values to vanish; the standard strongly additive function ω also fails that clause at k=0, p=2.
The shared strongly additive disjunct is incompatible with the other hypotheses, and the concrete positive-exponent power law for ω demonstrates why including k=0 changes its meaning.

not_demonstrated.reason: Its full bounded-gap statement is a nontrivial true consequence of Wirsing’s theorem, not a trivially false statement; examples separating its one-sided conclusion from a bounded residual do not satisfy the bounded-gap hypothesis and would not prove or refute the declaration as requested.

submission.summary: Created /workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean with short diagnostics of the exact inline hypotheses shared by four declarations. These are hypothesis demonstrations, not proofs or disproofs of the full conjectures. The required compile command completed with no errors or warnings.

trivial_proof.lean:
import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«897»

/-!
Diagnostics of the literal hypotheses in Erdős 897, not proofs of the full conjectures.
The two unrestricted parts share a growth hypothesis; the two variants share a power-law clause.
`Erdos897.erdos_897.variants.log_growth` is not demonstrated here: its full theorem is nontrivial.
-/

open Filter
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
namespace Erdos897Diagnostics

noncomputable def spike (n : ℕ) : ℝ := (n.factorization 2 : ℝ)^2

/-- Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.i and Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.ii:
The concrete test function v₂(n)² satisfies their literal additivity hypothesis. -/
example : ∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → spike (a*b) = spike a + spike b := by
  intro a ha b hb hc
  have hmin : min (a.factorization 2) (b.factorization 2) = 0 := by
    simpa [Nat.factorization_gcd ha.ne' hb.ne'] using
      congrArg (fun n : ℕ => n.factorization 2) hc.gcd_eq_one
  have hz : a.factorization 2 = 0 ∨ b.factorization 2 = 0 := by omega
  rcases hz with hz | hz <;> simp [spike, Nat.factorization_mul ha.ne' hb.ne', hz]

/-- Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.i and Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.ii:
This input has the intended unbounded prime-power growth, already along powers of 2. -/
example : Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => spike (2^k) / (2^k : ℝ).log) atTop atTop := by
  have h (k : ℕ) : spike (2^k) / (2^k : ℝ).log = (k : ℝ) / Real.log 2 := by
    simp [spike, Nat.factorization_pow, Nat.prime_two.factorization, Real.log_pow,
      pow_two, div_mul_eq_div_div, mul_self_div_self]
  simpa only [h] using
    (tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop : Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => (k : ℝ)) atTop atTop).atTop_div_const
      (Real.log_pos (by norm_num : (1 : ℝ) < 2))

/-- Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.i and Erdos897.erdos_897.parts.ii:
Their literal growth hypothesis nevertheless rejects this input: eventually p ≥ 3 erases the spike. -/
example : ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
    (fun (p, k) => (spike (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal))) ≠ ⊤ := by
  apply ne_of_lt
  refine lt_of_le_of_lt (b := (0 : EReal)) ?_ (by simp)
  apply Filter.limsup_le_of_le (by isBoundedDefault)
  rw [Filter.eventually_inf_principal]
  filter_upwards [Filter.eventually_ge_atTop ((3,0) : ℕ × ℕ)] with q hq hp
  have hneq : q.1 ≠ 2 := by have := hq.1; omega
  simp [spike, Nat.factorization_pow, hp.factorization, hneq]

/-- Erdos897.erdos_897.variants.parts.i and Erdos897.erdos_897.variants.parts.ii:
Their literal first disjunct is impossible under their additivity and growth hypotheses. -/
example (f : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hf : ∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b)
    (hg : ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤))
    (hs : ∀ k p, p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p) : False := by
  have h1 : f 1 = 0 := by simpa using hf 1 (by norm_num) 1 (by norm_num) (by simp)
  have hz (p k : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) : f (p^k) = 0 := by
    rw [hs k p hp, ← hs 0 p hp, pow_zero, h1]
  have hle : (Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) ≤ 0 := by
    apply Filter.limsup_le_of_le (by isBoundedDefault)
    rw [Filter.eventually_inf_principal]
    exact Filter.Eventually.of_forall fun ⟨p,k⟩ hp => by simp [hz p k hp]
  rw [hg] at hle
  exact (EReal.coe_lt_top 0).not_ge hle

noncomputable def distinctPrimeCount (n : ℕ) : ℝ := n.primeFactors.card

/-- Erdos897.erdos_897.variants.parts.i and Erdos897.erdos_897.variants.parts.ii:
Concretely, the standard strongly additive ω(n) obeys the positive-exponent law but fails the written one at k=0, p=2. -/
example : (∀ k p : ℕ, 0 < k → p.Prime →
      distinctPrimeCount (p^k) = distinctPrimeCount p) ∧
    ¬ (∀ k p, p.Prime → distinctPrimeCount (p^k) = distinctPrimeCount p) := by
  constructor
  · intro k p hk hp
    simp [distinctPrimeCount, Nat.primeFactors_pow p hk.ne']
  · intro h
    have h0 := h 0 2 Nat.prime_two
    norm_num [distinctPrimeCount] at h0

end Erdos897Diagnostics

/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p^k \to \infty} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$,
where $p$ is prime and $k\geq 1$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n f(n+1)/ f(n) = ∞$?

The answer is no; the same counterexample is formalised in Lean by Aristotle [ArWu25].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos897.lean"]
theorem erdos_897.parts.ii : answer(False) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b) →
    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}).limsup
      (fun q => (f q / (q : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => (f (n+1) / f n : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/--
Wirsing [Wi70] proved that if $|f(n+1)−f(n)| ≤ C$ then $f(n) = c \log n + O(1)$ for some constant
$c$. This is Erdős Problem 491; see `erdos_491`, whose linked formal proof gives this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos491.lean#L34"]
theorem erdos_897.variants.log_growth
    (f : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hf : ∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b)
    (C : ℝ) (hf' : ∀ n, |f (n+1) - f n| ≤ C) :
    ∃ c, ∃ (O : ℕ → ℝ), O =O[Filter.atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧
      ∀ n, f n = c*Real.log n + O n := by
  sorry


/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p^k \to \infty} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$,
where $p$ is prime and $k\geq 1$. Suppose either $f(p^k) = f(p)$ for all such $p,k$,
or $f(p^k) = kf(p)$ for all such $p,k$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n (f(n+1)−f(n))/ \log n = ∞$?

The known counterexample does not satisfy either of these extra hypotheses, so this variant remains
open.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_897.variants.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b) →
    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}).limsup
      (fun q => (f q / (q : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    (∀ (k p : ℕ), 0 < k → p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p) ∨
      (∀ (k p : ℕ), 0 < k → p.Prime → f (p^k) = k*f p) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => ((f (n+1) - f n) / (n : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry
